record.context_brief: Classification of fullerenes without gSW moves
record.original_question: A fullerene is a convex, 3-regular polytope consisting only of pentagonal and hexagonal facets. For a feasible n, meaning a positive even integer n >= 20 with n != 22, let T_n be the unique dual graph of such a fullerene. A generalized Stone-Wales (gSW) path in T_n is a path (v_1, ..., v_{2w}) of odd length 2w - 1 such that v_1 and v_{2w} have degree 5, v_2 and v_{2w-1} have degree 6, all vertices are distinct, and (v_i, v_{i+2}) is an edge for every i = 1, ..., 2w - 2. Since a gSW operation can be applied only when such a path exists, which fullerene isomers do not permit any generalized Stone-Wales operation at all?

evidence.quote: A fullerene is a convex, 3-regular polytope consisting only of pentagonal and hexagonal facets.
Thus, we define a positive even integer n ≥ 20, n ̸= 22, as feasible.

Since fullerenes are 3-connected, Whitney’s theorem cf. [25] ensures that their dual graph is unique. A dual fullerene, denoted by Tn , can also be viewed as an element of the set of all convex triangulations of the sphere, as described in [19].

Definition 1. For a feasible n and w ∈ N, w ≥ 2, let a Cn -isomer with dual graph Tn be given. We call (a) a path (v1 , . . . , v2w ) with vi ∈ V (Tn ) a gSW path of length 2w − 1, if the following in Tn holds: • v1 and v2w have degree 5, • v2 and v2w−1 have degree 6, • vi ̸= vj for i ̸= j, • (vi , vi+2 ) ∈ E (Tn ) for all i = 1, . . . , 2w − 2.
From this definition, it follows that the existence of a gSW path in a fullerene is necessary to apply the gSW operation to this fullerene.
Open Problem 2. Identify all fullerenes that do not permit a gSW operation.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A fullerene is a convex, 3-regular polytope all of whose facets are pentagons or hexagons. Call a positive even integer n feasible if n ≥ 20 and n ≠ 22; for every feasible n there exists at least one fullerene with exactly n vertices, and by Whitney's theorem the (planar) dual graph of any 3-connected polytope is unique. For a fullerene isomer on n vertices let T_n denote its dual graph; T_n is a triangulation of the sphere in which every vertex has degree 5 or 6, with exactly 12 vertices of degree 5.

For w ∈ ℕ with w ≥ 2, a generalized Stone–Wales (gSW) path of length 2w−1 in T_n is a sequence of pairwise distinct vertices (v_1, v_2, …, v_{2w}) of T_n such that:
  • deg(v_1) = deg(v_{2w}) = 5,
  • deg(v_2) = deg(v_{2w-1}) = 6,
  • {v_i, v_{i+2}} ∈ E(T_n) for every i = 1, …, 2w−2.

A gSW operation can be performed on a fullerene isomer if and only if its dual graph T_n contains at least one gSW path.

Problem: Classify all fullerene isomers (equivalently, all dual fullerene graphs T_n over feasible n) that contain no gSW path, i.e. those isomers on which no generalized Stone–Wales operation can be applied.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is listed among open mathematical problems on fullerenes. It is known that infinitely many fullerene isomers admit no gSW operation, and only one such isomer is known on fewer than 70 vertices, but a complete classification of fullerene isomers without any gSW path has not been established.

status_evidence.title: Some Open Mathematical Problems on Fullerenes
status_evidence.snippet: Infinitely many fullerene isomers cannot be generated by any sequence of gSW operations; only one isomer with fewer than 70 vertices lacks a gSW path. A proper classification of such fullerenes is sought.
status_evidence.claim: Classification of fullerene isomers admitting no gSW operation is stated as an open problem.

status_evidence.title: Generalized Stone-Wales Transformations
status_evidence.snippet: Generalized Stone-Wales transformations were introduced as rearrangements generalizing the classical Stone-Wales flip, allowing generation of fullerene isomer spaces.
status_evidence.claim: Defines gSW transformations relevant to the problem.
